fields.foundation: The Songhai Empire was the largest empire in West African history and reached its height in the late fifteenth and sixteenth centuries under Sunni Ali and Askia Muhammad. Its origins are much older. Songhai-speaking peoples had lived on the bend of the Niger River around Gao since at least the ninth century CE, and a Songhai kingdom under the Za dynasty (or Dia dynasty) was for a time a tributary of the Mali Empire. The Sunni or Sonni dynasty, which by tradition threw off Malian overlordship in the fourteenth century, produced the ruler who built the empire. Sunni Ali (r. 1464–1492) was a highly capable military commander, and his campaigns turned a modest Sahelian kingdom into an empire. His first great success was the Songhai conquest of Timbuktu in 1468, taken from the Tuareg who had held it since Mali's decline. His second was the trading city of Djenné in the inland delta, which, according to tradition, resisted the Siege of Djenné for seven years before submitting around 1473. With these two cities Songhai controlled the most important centres of trans-Saharan commerce and Islamic scholarship in West Africa. Sunni Ali died in 1492, reportedly by drowning while crossing a river in flood. In 1493 Muhammad Ture, one of his leading commanders and a devout Muslim, defeated Sunni Ali's son Sunni Baru in a coup and took the title Askia. Askia Muhammad's pilgrimage to Mecca (1496–1498), during which the Abbasid shadow caliph in Cairo recognised him as his deputy in the western Sudan, gave the empire a religious legitimacy that Sunni Ali's syncretic rule had never had, and it opened the empire's golden age.
fields.socioeconomy: The Songhai economy rested on the farming of the Niger Inland Delta, the trans-Saharan gold and salt trade, and the commercial revenues of the great cities, Gao, Timbuktu and Djenné, which were the empire's centres of commerce and learning. The Niger's annual flood covered the inland delta for several months each year and left rich alluvial soils. These supported intensive cultivation of rice, sorghum and millet, and the surpluses fed large urban populations and a substantial workforce that did not farm. The gold trade carried gold from the goldfields to the south and west through Songhai territory to Moroccan and North African markets, in exchange for salt from the Taghaza mines and Mediterranean luxury goods, and it brought the imperial treasury large customs revenues. Timbuktu was the empire's showpiece. Leo Africanus, the Granada-born traveller raised in Fez, visited around 1510 and described a wealthy city where books were sold at greater profit than any other merchandise and where scholars gathered around the Sankore mosque. Royal estates worked by servile labour, many of them hereditary dependants of the crown, produced grain for the court and army. Long-distance trade relied on established weights, measures and merchant networks, with Wangara (Dyula) merchants as the principal long-distance intermediaries. The economy's chief weakness was its dependence on trans-Saharan routes, which political instability in the Sahara and the Maghreb could disrupt.
fields.military: The Songhai military combined a professional core with large contingents drawn from subject peoples, and its methods of expansion were those of Sunni Ali. Its most distinctive element was the Niger River fleet, a corps of war canoes crewed by specialists from the Sorko fishing communities, who had worked the Niger for centuries. On the waterways of the Niger Bend the fleet gave Songhai a decisive advantage: it could move troops quickly and supply them by river, which opponents on land could not match. The cavalry, drawn from the Songhai nobility and allied peoples, was the mobile striking force for campaigns in the Sahel and along the desert edge, while infantry from subject agricultural peoples supplied the numbers needed for sieges. Sunni Ali campaigned with great speed and was politically ruthless. He treated Timbuktu's scholars harshly, regarding them as politically subversive, and the hostile chronicles that resulted still colour the historical record against him. Askia Muhammad created a standing army of full-time soldiers and appointed military commanders such as the balama, while the hi-koy commanded the river fleet; he led campaigns against the Mossi in 1498 and against Aïr and the Hausa states in the early sixteenth century. The Moroccan invasion of 1591 exposed the empire's military weakness. The Sa'adian sultan Ahmad al-Mansur sent an expeditionary force of around 4,000 men across the Sahara, armed with arquebuses and light cannon that the Songhai cavalry and infantry, however numerous, could not withstand. At the Battle of Tondibi a much larger Songhai army was routed in a single engagement, which showed how far gunpowder weapons could favour a small, well-equipped force over a larger army armed in the older way.
fields.governance: Songhai government combined the administrative inheritance of the Mali Empire with innovations of Askia Muhammad that made the empire more centralised than its predecessor. The empire was divided into provinces under governors bearing titles such as fari or farma, often royal kinsmen or trusted commanders rather than local hereditary chiefs. The most senior was the kurmina-fari, who governed the western provinces. This was a departure from Mali's more indirect rule and gave Songhai greater cohesion over its territorial core. Askia Muhammad kept a formal court protocol in which subjects prostrated themselves before the ruler and sprinkled dust on their heads, rituals that combined West African royal ceremony with elements of Islamic court tradition. Islamic qadis administered Islamic law in the towns, and customary legal systems served the largely non-Muslim rural population, so that the empire had two bodies of law for its two religious communities. Timbuktu and Djenné had arrangements of their own. They were governed through negotiation between imperial appointees and the Islamic scholarly and merchant elites, without whose cooperation commerce could not function; in Timbuktu the qadi exercised wide authority. Timbuktu's scholarly community, centred on the Sankore mosque and supported by imperial patronage, produced learning of international standing. The jurist Ahmad Baba al-Timbukti, whose works survive in manuscript, belonged to the tradition that made Timbuktu synonymous with scholarship across the Islamic world. The empire's chief administrative weakness was royal succession. After Askia Muhammad was deposed by his son Askia Musa in 1528, a series of violent successions destabilised the administration and diverted military resources to internal conflict. They ended in the civil war of 1588, which left the empire divided as the Moroccan threat developed.
fields.impact: The Songhai Empire was the high point of West African political and commercial development in the pre-colonial era. It showed that African societies could build large states with developed administrations that held diverse populations together across great distances. It controlled the trans-Saharan trade at a period of intense activity and so connected West African gold and other goods to North African, Mediterranean and Middle Eastern markets. West African gold circulated through the Ottoman, Mamluk and European monetary systems and affected commercial conditions across the connected world. Timbuktu's learning is preserved in manuscripts, many of which survive in private family libraries in modern Mali. They form one of the most substantial bodies of pre-colonial African scholarship and cover Islamic jurisprudence, astronomy, mathematics, medicine and history. The great Timbuktu chronicles, the Tarikh al-Sudan and Tarikh al-Fattash, written in the seventeenth century, preserve the memory of Songhai itself. The empire's administration of diverse peoples set precedents that influenced the Moroccan-controlled pashalik of Timbuktu that succeeded it and later states of the western Sudan. The Moroccan destruction of the Songhai state in 1591 was, from a broad historical perspective, a severe interruption of West African political development. The Moroccan occupation failed to establish an effective replacement administration, trans-Saharan trade was disrupted, and the political fragmentation that followed prevented the emergence of a comparable large-scale state in the Niger Bend for generations. Insecurity and the breakdown of order along the river damaged the agricultural systems that had made the region productive, with lasting demographic consequences for the Sahel.
fields.decline: The Songhai Empire collapsed suddenly, under attack from outside. The immediate cause was Morocco's invasion of 1591. The Sa'adian sultan Ahmad al-Mansur was determined to control the source of the trans-Saharan gold trade, and he timed the invasion to exploit the civil war that had divided Songhai since 1588. His expeditionary force of around 4,000 soldiers, largely Andalusian Morisco and European renegade arquebusiers together with Moroccan troops, crossed the Sahara under the command of Judar Pasha, himself a Spanish-born convert. It was one of the boldest military operations in African history, and the force lost a substantial part of its strength to thirst and heat on the march. At the Battle of Tondibi on 13 March 1591, the Songhai army assembled by Askia Ishaq II, estimated variously at between about 12,500 and 40,000 men, was routed by sustained arquebus and cannon fire. A herd of cattle that the Songhai reportedly drove towards the Moroccan lines stampeded back into their own ranks, and the Songhai cavalry, unable to close with their opponents under concentrated fire, disintegrated. The Moroccans occupied Gao and Timbuktu soon afterwards. Devastation followed, not an orderly change of rulers. The Moroccan administration could not govern the wide Songhai territories effectively, the gold it expected to seize proved largely out of reach in distant goldfields, and trans-Saharan trade suffered from the insecurity created by the conquest. The Songhai royal family retreated south-east and maintained an independent state in Dendi for generations, but the integrated system of commerce and administration on which the empire had rested was broken beyond repair. By the early seventeenth century the Niger Bend had fragmented into competing polities, with the descendants of the Moroccan soldiers, the Arma, ruling Timbuktu. The region's population and economic output did not recover to pre-conquest levels for generations.
fields.summary: The Songhai Empire was the greatest state of pre-colonial West Africa, and its government, commerce and scholarship showed what African states could achieve. In 1591 a small Moroccan army destroyed it suddenly, because its gunpowder weapons outmatched a much larger force.
fields.teaser: The largest empire in West African history, Songhai ruled from its capital Gao, while Timbuktu flourished as a centre of trade and Islamic learning.
fields.t0: The largest empire in West African history, Songhai controlled the Niger Bend and its trade cities of Gao, Timbuktu and Djenné.
fields.t1: Its wealth came from the trans-Saharan gold and salt trade, and its patronage made Timbuktu a centre of Islamic scholarship.
fields.t2: Weakened by civil war, it was shattered in 1591 by a small Moroccan army whose firearms routed a far larger Songhai force at Tondibi.
fields.dyk: The traveller Leo Africanus, visiting Timbuktu around 1510, reported that books were sold there at greater profit than any other merchandise.
